external_evidence.finding: The results of the prospective randomized trials conﬁrm that MKI leads to improved PFS compared to placebo for ﬁrst-line RAI-refractory DTC, and likely also provide beneﬁt in patients with PDTC or DHGTC. In particular, lenvatinib has a moderate quality of evidence supporting its use, given more impressive PFS beneﬁt compared to sorafenib or vandetanib. Thus, for patients with driver mutation–negative PDTC or DHGTC with RAI-refractory and progressive disease re- quiring systemic therapy, lenvatinib or sorafenib may be considered. Lenvatinib with pembrolizumab may be con- sidered for patients with aggressive PDTC or DHGTC, but there is insufﬁcient evidence to formally recommend this strategy. Recommendation 5.2 Literature review and analysis. The literature review did not yield any prospective or retrospective studies of MKI in the subsequent-line setting speciﬁcally for PDTC or DHGTC. COSMIC-311, 73 which established cabozantinib as second- line therapy, RAI-refractory, differentiated thyroid cancer, included fewer than 10 patients with PDTC and thus did not meet criteria for inclusion as part of the evidence base for this guideline. Clinical interpretation.

The results of prospective, ran- domized, placebo-controlled studies conﬁrm the beneﬁt o f treatment with multikinase TKIs in patients with RAI- refractory, well-differentiated thyroid cancer. Most pa- tients who require treatment for their disease are symp- tomatic and need a reduction in tumor burden. Since the response rates for lenvatinib are almost three times that of sorafenib, lenvatinib is generally the preferred ﬁrst-line agent. Similarly, PFS is longer with lenvatinib. However, head-to-head studies comparing the efﬁcacy of these two agents are lacking. Both lenvatinib and sorafenib were as- sociated with signiﬁcant adverse effects that often led to dose reductions and discontinuation of therapy in their respective randomized, placebo-controlled trials. external_evidence.finding: The results of the prospective randomized trials conﬁrm that MKI leads to improved PFS compared to placebo for ﬁrst-line RAI-refractory DTC, and likely also provide beneﬁt in patients with PDTC or DHGTC. Thus, for patients with driver mutation–negative PDTC or DHGTC with RAI-refractory and progressive disease re- quiring systemic therapy, lenvatinib or sorafenib may be considered. Lenvatinib with pembrolizumab may be con- sidered for patients with aggressive PDTC or DHGTC, but there is insufﬁcient evidence to formally recommend this strategy. Recommendation 5.2 Literature review and analysis. The literature review did not yield any prospective or retrospective studies of MKI in the subsequent-line setting speciﬁcally for PDTC or DHGTC. COSMIC-311, 73 which established cabozantinib as second- line therapy, RAI-refractory, differentiated thyroid cancer, included fewer than 10 patients with PDTC and thus did not meet criteria for inclusion as part of the evidence base for this guideline. Clinical interpretation.

guideline_evidence.finding: best practices for prevention, screening, palliative and supportive care, and disease management of cancer. In the United States, many patients remain unable to reap the beneﬁts of innovative prevention and early detection programs, biomarker testing, and new cancer therapies due to challenges including lack of transportation, stable housing, adequate insurance coverage, food insecurity, health literacy, proximity to a dedicated cancer center, and cost of treatment and other services. 94 Additionally, some populations experience stigma along with barriers to cancer screening, prevention, and treatment that contribute to these cancer disparities. 95 Further, geographic disparities can also impact the quality- of-care patients receive. Rural patients are more likely to have worse survivorship outcomes and experience higher mortality rates compared to nonrural patients. This can be attributed, in part, to a lower density of specialists and dedicated cancer centers, as only 21% of nonmetropolitan counties in the United States have one or more practicing oncologists.

guideline_evidence.finding: Furthermore, access to the necessary systemic therapy medications, including MKIs, may vary based on treatment location. Finally, many thyroid malignancies are rare; expertise in management is not universal and may impact care. Overall, there is signiﬁcant opportunity to improve access to swift diagnosis, high-quality pathological diagnosis, and expertise in multidisciplinary treatment of thyroid carci- nomas to improve patient care. MULTIPLE CHRONIC CONDITIONS Creating evidence-based recommendations to inform treat- ment of patients with additional chronic conditions, a situa- tion in which the patient may have two or more such conditions—referred to as multiple chronic conditions (MCC)—is challenging. Patients with MCC are a complex and heterogeneous population, making it difﬁcult to account for all of the possible permutations to develop speciﬁc recommen- dations for care. In addition, the best available evidence for treating index conditions, such as cancer, is often from clinical trials whose study selection criteria may exclude these patients in order to avoid potential interaction effects or confounding of results associated with MCC.
